# On the Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about my grandmother's garden, which she abandoned sometime around 2003. Not abandoned in the dramatic sense—she didn't flee in the night or lose interest overnight. Rather, she simply stopped weeding one summer and never quite resumed. By the time I visited a few years later, the boundary between garden and wild had become negotiable.

There was something deeply honest about that space. The tomato plants had found their way into the perennials. Mint had colonized three-quarters of a bed. Actual interesting wildflowers that nobody planted were thriving next to the roses. And instead of the neat rows I remember from childhood, where everything was precisely where my grandmother had calculated it should be, there was this gorgeous chaos—which somehow seemed more alive than the manicured version had been.

This image keeps returning to me when I think about why we're so uncomfortable with incompleteness.

We're obsessed with finished things. Completed projects. Resolved narratives. The satisfying snap of a book's conclusion, the final credit roll, the before-and-after transformation. There's a reason the phrase "closure" has become so prominent in our psychological vocabulary. We crave it. We organize our lives around it. Unfinished business, we say, as though it's a problem requiring solution rather than perhaps just a permanent condition of being alive.

But I wonder if we've lost something in this drive toward completion.

I think about the artists I've read about who say they have to actively stop themselves from working on a painting, because there's no natural endpoint—only the point where they force themselves to step away. I think about how the best conversations rarely have conclusions, they just fade out naturally as people drift apart. I think about how gardens, left to their own devices, actually become more biodiverse, more resilient, more genuinely flourishing than the ones where every variable is controlled.

The unfinished things in my life right now are numerous and they stress me out in fairly regular intervals. A half-written novel that's been sitting untouched for eight months. A relationship that ended without proper resolution—we just slowly stopped calling. A argument with my brother that we've agreed not to revisit, which means it's technically resolved but emotionally unfinished. A degree I started but abandoned. A degree I finished but haven't quite processed. A list of house repairs that grows faster than I can tackle it. Dreams I've set aside but can't quite relinquish.

For a long time, these things felt like failures. Like evidence of my incomplete nature, my inability to see things through, my fundamental lack of follow-through. But I've been gradually reconsidering.

What if unfinished things are actually where the living happens?

An unfinished novel still gets to exist in the realm of pure possibility. It could become anything. It could be the greatest thing I ever write or the thing I finally abandon, and honestly, both options are interesting in their own way. The moment you finish something, you kill possibility. You're committed now. You've made your statement and you're stuck with it.

The relationships that ended without resolution still teach me something new every time I think about them. They're not locked down, filed away, neatly explained. They remain open to reinterpretation. Maybe in five years I'll have enough distance to understand what actually happened. Maybe I never will, and that's okay. The person I was then and the person I am now can both inhabit the same unfinished story.

I wonder if some of my anxiety about unfinished things comes from the culture we've built, where productivity is god and completion is proof of worth. You can't tell someone you're "working on yourself" without it sounding vaguely absurd, as though the self is a project with a deadline. We want to be finished. Done. Perfected. But people aren't products. Gardens aren't either.

There's an Czesław Miłosz poem where he talks about the nature of time, and how we cling to each moment as though it's discrete and finished, when really time is all one thing, flowing and interconnected. Every moment contains all the moments that came before it and influence all the moments to come. Nothing is ever truly finished because nothing ever truly ends—it just flows into whatever comes next.

Maybe that's why incomplete things feel sacred to me now.

My grandmother eventually sold that house. Someone else bought it and presumably tended the garden back into submission, or maybe they let it become something new. I'll never know. But I carry that image with me—not as a failure of maintenance but as a kind of rebellion. A space where she stopped insisting on control and let something else have a say in what grew there.

I think I want my life to have more of that quality. More willingness to let things be partially done, partially known, partially resolved. More trust in the idea that loose threads aren't failures—they're potential. They're the places where the world gets to surprise you.

This piece itself is unfinished in some ways. There's no neat conclusion I'm building toward. I won't resolve the tensions I've raised or provide you with a satisfying ending that ties everything back together. There's just this—these thoughts, released into the world in this particular configuration, never to be written exactly this way again, already beginning their journey into whatever meaning you'll find in them.

And I think that might be exactly as it should be.
